name: Webhooks
intent: Let one system push events to another over HTTP as they happen, instead of making the receiver ask over and over.
scenario: A payment provider tells a shop when a payment succeeds, by sending an HTTP request to the shop's webhook URL. The shop then marks the order as paid and ships it.
problem: Polling an API to find out whether something changed wastes calls and is always a little late. Pushing events solves that, but now the sender is calling a server it does not control: that server can be down, slow, or attacked with fake events, and the same event may arrive more than once.

howItWorks.title: Register a URL and subscribe to events
howItWorks.text: The receiver gives the sender an HTTPS endpoint and chooses which event types it wants (payment.succeeded, order.shipped). When something happens, the sender makes a POST request to that URL with a small JSON body describing the event.

howItWorks.title: Acknowledge fast, process later
howItWorks.text: The receiver should answer 2xx within a few seconds and do the real work asynchronously, for example by putting the event on a queue. A slow handler makes the sender think delivery failed and send it again.

howItWorks.title: Verify the sender
howItWorks.text: Anyone can post to a public URL. The sender signs each request, typically an HMAC of the timestamp and body using a shared secret, and puts the signature in a header. The receiver recomputes it and rejects mismatches, and rejects old timestamps to stop replayed requests.

howItWorks.title: Retry on failure, with backoff
howItWorks.text: If the endpoint returns an error or does not answer, the sender retries on a schedule that grows (for example after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours), then gives up and often disables the endpoint. A receiver that was down for an hour should still catch up.

howItWorks.title: Expect duplicates and out-of-order delivery
howItWorks.text: Retries mean the same event can arrive twice, and events can arrive out of order. Every event carries a unique id. The receiver records ids it has handled and ignores repeats, so processing is idempotent, and it treats the event as a hint to fetch current state when order matters.

pros: Far fewer wasted API calls on both sides
Simple to integrate: it is just an HTTP endpoint
Decouples the sender from the receiver's internals
cons: The receiver must expose a public, secured endpoint
Delivery is at least once, so duplicates and reordering happen
Receivers that are down miss events until retries succeed, or forever if retries run out
Hard to test and debug locally without tools
whenToUse: Notifying other systems about events: payments, shipments, repository pushes
Replacing polling loops that check for changes
whenNotToUse: Very high-volume streams, where a message broker or streaming API fits better
When the receiver cannot expose an endpoint or needs guaranteed ordering
Large payloads: send an event with an id and let the receiver fetch the details
pitfalls: Trusting the request without verifying its signature
Doing slow work before replying, which triggers needless retries
Not deduplicating on event id, so a retry ships the order twice
Assuming events arrive in order or that none are ever missed (reconcile occasionally by listing events)

roles.label: Sender
roles.description: Detects events and delivers them with a signature.

roles.label: Webhook endpoint
roles.description: Verifies, acknowledges and hands off the event.

roles.label: Worker
roles.description: Does the real work after the acknowledgement.
